title: From Regulation to Behaviour Change: Giving Nudge the Third Degree
abstract: Behaviour change strategies such as ‘nudge’ have become hugely popular with administrations on both sides of the Atlantic. The practice of nudging, however, raises conceptual and controversial issues which must be addressed in examining the conditions under which nudging can be used effectively and acceptably. A key to a clear conceptual understanding of nudge‐related issues is to distinguish between three degrees of nudge. These three degrees raise different, and identifiable, concerns and it is possible to assess the extent to which these can be responded to in positive terms. The compatibility of nudging with other control devices cannot be assumed and, when contemplating nudging, it is essential to be transparent about its philosophical basis, as well as to be aware that different modes of intervention may operate with clashes of logic that threaten not only effectiveness but also the serving of representative and ethical ends.

claims.text: Nudge interventions can be conceptually categorized into three degrees based on their impact on individual decision-making autonomy.
First Degree nudges respect decision-making autonomy and enhance conscious, reflective decision-making.
Second Degree nudges exploit behavioural or volitional limitations to bias choices while remaining uncoverable upon reflection.
Third Degree nudges involve framing strategies, emotional affect, or covert mechanisms that materially obstruct conscious reflection.
The degree of a nudge intervention is distinct from the specific nudging tool deployed.
Nudges targeting individual decision-making are ineffective as sole interventions when problems stem from collective, structural, or environmental causes.
Second and Third Degree nudges can undermine relationships of trust when targets uncover that they are being paternalistically manipulated.
Opt-out mechanisms in nudging discriminate against individuals with lower cognitive capacity, fewer resources, or vulnerable positions.
The cumulative burden of multiple nudges degrades overall individual autonomy over time.
Combining nudges with traditional regulatory mechanisms creates clashes of regulatory logic that can undermine the effectiveness of both.

limitations.text: Empirical evidence regarding the impact and effectiveness profiles of different nudge tools across varied target capacities and intentions remains thin on the ground.
It is difficult to state in precise terms the exact universal conditions under which nudging can be deployed both effectively and acceptably.
Prior nudge scholarship and policymaking adopt overly broad definitions of nudge that conflate conscious think strategies with automated System 1 manipulations.
There is a paucity of empirical studies demonstrating that significant population-level behaviour change can be achieved by non-regulatory nudge strategies alone.

future_work.text: Governments need to establish rigorous and broad-based empirical studies specifically designed to evaluate behaviour change interventions.

methodologies.name: Three degrees of nudge conceptual taxonomy
methodologies.description: A conceptual framework categorizing behavioural change interventions into three distinct degrees according to their degree of impact on personal autonomy and capacity for reflection.
